Nous-Volition · Streams and Rocks · SIMS study · 9 October 2026 UTC

SIMS: names, memory, and group boundaries

Do boundaries come from names, remembered relationships, or the arrangement?

SIMS are the simulated participants in this six-group experiment.

Names alone did nothing to these SIMS. Explicit identity preferences and remembered interactions changed their choices. Stress reduced cooperation, but did not automatically strengthen group boundaries.

This is a social analogy. Ice, Water, Fog, Mist, Gas (water vapor), and Smoke are symbolic labels. Fog and mist contain suspended liquid droplets; Smoke is not a water phase. This study has no fluid or molecular equations and identifies no new physical law.

Actually executed: 6,444 main and control trajectories; 72 later diagnostic trajectories; 144 copying-influence assays; 288 synthetic attribution assays; and 35,928 group shuffles. Each trajectory contains 120 rounds. The core has 60 SIMS; sensitivity runs use 30 and 120. Three network arrangements and equal/unequal groups were tested. Twelve discovery seeds and twelve independent replication seeds were used. No humans participated.

Intervals are descriptive 95% bootstrap intervals across 12 independent seeds, with matched conditions averaged within seed. Thousands of trajectories are not thousands of independent experimental units. The intervals cover simulation sampling variability, not uncertainty about human psychology or the model's assumptions.

Stress did not simply “freeze the tribes”

In the full model, cooperation fell from 83.94% in the matched no-stress condition to 65.51% during stress. Same-group choice above its available-partner share fell from 16.76 to 7.26 percentage points. Fewer visible candidates constrained the expression of an unchanged identity preference; an opportunity adjustment does not remove that constraint. The component tests identify which implemented changes produced these effects.

Rigidity is an explicit adaptation variable driven by unsuccessful interactions. It rose during stress. In the last ten recovery rounds, the residual rigidity difference was +0.023 [+0.021, +0.025] with memory and +0.006 [+0.006, +0.007] without it. Same-group choice had no clear late residual difference. This is temporary persistence within 40 recovery rounds, not proof of permanent group rigidity or hysteresis.

Only 5 of 72 memory-enabled pairs met the strict joint recovery rule by round 120; 44 of 72 did so without memory. The rule requires two consecutive ten-round blocks within 0.03 of the paired no-stress condition for both rigidity and choice excess. These pairs are clustered within twelve seeds. The horizon was too short to estimate unrestricted mean recovery time; censored cases remain censored.

Stress components, population size, and parameter sensitivity

Smoke, exclusion, and alliances

Smoke had no special causal status when words were inert. Assigning any label an avoidance coefficient of −0.7 reduced nominations to that label; targeting Smoke reduced incoming choices by 0.421 per member per round [0.383, 0.463]. Comparable effects appeared when each other label was targeted. This demonstrates the imposed bias mechanism, not an observed human dislike of Smoke.

A separate fictional attribution exercise gives all six labels identical failure evidence. Adding a prior favoring blame creates excess blame by construction. Neither that assay nor the cooperation model discovers scapegoating. In the full model, the combined-stress change in ten-round nonselection was small and its interval included zero. Forty-round cooperation networks remained connected in the main factorial runs. Strong reciprocal cross-group ties were measured as alliance proxies; no coalition bargaining or intent was modeled.

Does leadership belong to a person or the arrangement?

Identical agents on a regular ring had equal copying-response influence. Random and hub arrangements generated unequal scores. Exchanging the highest- and lowest-scoring identities left site scores unchanged for identical agents: the score moved with the site. This is a controlled symmetry demonstration, much like the earlier project's positional influence control. A separate assay added individual attraction and moved it with the individual.

The defensible answer is conditional: arrangement alone can create unequal influence in this model; individual differences can also matter when supplied. A copying-response score is not leadership, authority, or evidence about real human populations. One exploratory ring-network modularity null had a small negative interval excluding zero; the opportunity-adjusted random-choice null included zero. These finite-seed, multiple-diagnostic fluctuations do not overturn the exact lexical invariance control.

What remains proposed

The optional group-decision game is a separate proposal for volunteers and has not been run or registered. Its protocol specifies consent, neutral and evocative labels plus a hidden-group control, session-level randomization, a displayed-history manipulation, mild resource/time constraints, outcomes, exclusions, analysis, debriefing, and a fixed stopping rule. Behavioral-role and affiliation-change modules are future extensions. Longer recovery, alternate learning rules, and empirical calibration are also future work.

Checks: 12 unit tests passed; 18 selected trajectories reproduced exactly; all resource, group-accounting, source-hash, and saved-result checks passed. The simulation plan was saved before the ensemble. Detailed analysis and the additional diagnostics were developed afterward, so this report is exploratory, not a retrospectively claimed preregistration.

Sources: Tajfel et al. (1971), arbitrary categorization; Newman (2003), assortative mixing; Grimm et al. (2020), documenting agent-based models. These motivate design and measurement; none calibrates this simulation.
